title: How animals move, and how their mouths fit their food

summary.text: A frog's back legs are longer than the rest of her body, but they stay folded up until she jumps. Animals move by pushing on something: legs push on the ground, wings push on air, and fins and webbed feet push on water. Snakes and earthworms have no legs, so they push with their whole body. Your child tests how far they can jump with straight legs, a small bend and a big bend in the knees. Then they find out how teeth and beaks fit the food each animal eats, from a cow's grinding teeth to a kingfisher's long, sharp beak.
summary.art: A city flat corridor with a girl crouched to jump at a dupatta start line, and in a bubble beside her a small brown frog with long back legs folded under her body.

intro.hook: A frog sitting still looks as if she has short legs. Then she jumps, and her back legs open out longer than her whole body. Where were those long legs hiding, and why do they fold up like that?
intro.text: Every animal that moves has to push on something. A crow's wings push on the air. A fish's tail pushes on the water. Your feet push on the floor. Animals also have mouths shaped for their food: sharp beaks, flat teeth, pointed teeth or no teeth at all. In this unit you test your own jump, crawl like a snake, flap like a bird, and grind a leaf the way a cow chews grass.
intro.art: A small brown frog shown twice: sitting with back legs folded small under her body, and in mid-jump with long back legs stretched out behind.

outcomes: By the end I can name how different animals move: with legs, wings, fins, or their whole body.
By the end I can explain that legs push on the ground, and that bent knees give a longer push and a longer jump.
By the end I can say how wings push on air, and how fins and webbed feet push on water.
By the end I can say how a snake and an earthworm move without legs.
By the end I can name cutting, pointed and grinding teeth, and match teeth to the food an animal eats.
By the end I can match a bird's beak to the food that bird eats.

terms.meaning: A joint is a place where two bones meet, so the body can bend there.
terms.example: Your knee, your elbow and your ankle are joints. A frog's long back legs have joints too.
terms.art: A child's leg bent at the knee, with the knee and ankle circled.

terms.meaning: A muscle is a part of the body that gets shorter to pull on a bone and move it.
terms.example: When you straighten your bent knee, the big muscle on the front of your thigh is pulling.
terms.art: A simple drawing of a bent leg with the thigh muscle coloured red.

terms.meaning: To jump is to push hard on the ground with your legs, so that your whole body leaves the ground.
terms.example: A frog, a cat, a grasshopper and you all jump by bending the legs first, then straightening them fast.
terms.art: A grasshopper in mid-jump, with the long back legs stretched out straight.

terms.meaning: A wing is a body part that pushes on the air, so an animal can fly.
terms.example: A crow, a bat and a butterfly all have wings. A bat's wing is skin stretched over long finger bones.
terms.art: Three wings side by side: a crow's feathered wing, a bat's skin wing and a butterfly's wing.

terms.meaning: A fin is a flat body part that a fish uses to push on water, to steer and to keep steady.
terms.example: A rohu fish swings her tail fin from side to side to swim forward.
terms.art: A silver rohu fish from the side, with the tail fin and side fins coloured.

terms.meaning: Webbed feet have thin skin stretched between the toes, like a paddle.
terms.example: Ducks and frogs have webbed feet, which push hard on water when they swim.
terms.art: A duck's orange foot spread open, showing the skin between the three front toes.

terms.meaning: To crawl is to move along with the body low and close to the ground.
terms.example: An earthworm crawls. A baby crawls on hands and knees. A snake slides along on the belly.
terms.art: An earthworm, a snake and a crawling baby in a row on the ground.

terms.meaning: To glide is to move through the air without flapping, by spreading out flat.
terms.example: The flying lizard of the Western Ghats spreads flaps of skin and glides from one tree to the next.
terms.art: A small lizard gliding between two tree trunks with orange skin flaps spread out at the sides.

terms.meaning: A beak is the hard mouth of a bird. Birds have beaks and no teeth.
terms.example: A sparrow's short, thick beak cracks seeds. A kingfisher's long, sharp beak grabs fish.
terms.art: A sparrow's head and a kingfisher's head side by side, showing their different beaks.

terms.meaning: Incisors are the thin, flat teeth at the front of the mouth. They cut and bite off food.
terms.example: You use your incisors to bite a piece off a guava or a banana.
terms.art: A child's smile with the front cutting teeth coloured blue.

terms.meaning: Canines are the pointed teeth beside the front teeth. They grip and tear food.
terms.example: A tiger's long canines grip and tear meat. Your own canines are small and pointed.
terms.art: A tiger's open mouth with the four long pointed canines coloured yellow.

terms.meaning: Molars are the wide, bumpy teeth at the back of the mouth. They grind food into small bits.
terms.example: A cow grinds grass with her big flat molars. You grind roti and rice with yours.
terms.art: A cow's back teeth, wide and flat, next to a child's back teeth.

terms.meaning: A herbivore eats plants. A carnivore eats other animals. An omnivore eats both.
terms.example: A cow is a herbivore. A tiger is a carnivore. A crow, a bear and most humans are omnivores.
terms.art: Three plates: grass and leaves for a cow, meat for a tiger, and rice, vegetables and fish for a girl.

explanations.context: This card is about what legs do when an animal walks, runs or jumps.
explanations.definition: Legs move a body by pushing back and down on the ground. The ground pushes back, and the body moves forward and up.
explanations.description: A leg is made of bones joined at joints, such as the knee. Muscles pull on the bones to bend and straighten the leg. When a leg straightens against the ground, the ground pushes the body the other way. A bent leg can push for longer than a straight one, and a longer push gives a faster start.
examples: When you walk, each foot pushes back on the floor, and you move forward.
On a slippery floor your foot slides back, so the push is lost and you hardly move.
A cat crouches low before jumping onto a wall, so her legs can push for longer.
explanations.art: A girl walking, with a small arrow from her foot pushing back on the floor and a bigger arrow showing her body moving forward.

explanations.context: This card is about animals whose legs are made for jumping, and how they do it.
explanations.definition: Jumping animals have long back legs that fold up when resting and straighten very fast to push off.
explanations.description: A frog's back legs fold in three parts under her body, like a letter Z. When she jumps, they all straighten at once. Because the legs are long, they keep pushing on the ground for longer. A grasshopper's big back legs work like a stretched rubber band: they store up energy, then let it go all at once.
examples: A frog's back legs, opened out, are longer than her head and body together.
A grasshopper's big back legs make the jump. The four smaller legs are for walking.
A cat, a goat and you bend your knees before every jump.
explanations.art: A frog shown twice: folded small in a Z shape, then stretched out in mid-jump.

explanations.context: This card is about how birds, bats and insects use wings.
explanations.definition: A wing flies by pushing air down and back. The air pushes the wing up and forward, and that holds the animal up.
explanations.description: On the way down, a bird spreads the wing wide and flat, so the wing pushes a lot of air. On the way up, many birds bend the wing in a little, so it pushes less air the wrong way. A bird's wing is covered in feathers. A bat's wing is skin stretched over very long finger bones, and a butterfly has four thin wings.
examples: A pigeon claps her wings loudly as she takes off.
A black kite circles high over the city, hardly flapping, on rising warm air.
A fruit bat flies at dusk on wings made of skin.
explanations.art: A crow from the side shown twice: wing spread wide and pushing down, then wing bent in and lifting up.

explanations.context: This card is about animals who travel through the air without flapping.
explanations.definition: A glider spreads out a wide, flat body or skin and falls slowly forward through the air, without flapping.
explanations.description: A flat, wide shape pushes on a lot of air as the animal falls, so the fall is slow and goes forward. In the forests of the Western Ghats, the flying lizard spreads flaps of skin held out on long ribs and glides between trees. The flying snake of India flattens her whole body and glides from a high branch. Flying fish glide above the sea on big, spread-out fins.
examples: A flying lizard can glide from one tree to another tree several metres away.
A flying snake makes her body flat and wide before she leaps.
A flying fish leaps out of the sea and glides on fins spread like wings.
explanations.art: A flying snake gliding between two trees, with her body flattened into a wavy ribbon.

explanations.concept: Swimming with fins and webbed feet
explanations.context: This card is about how animals push on water to swim.
explanations.definition: Swimmers move by pushing water backwards with a tail, fins, flippers or webbed feet.
explanations.description: A fish bends her body from side to side, and her tail fin pushes water back. The other fins steer and keep her steady. A duck spreads her toes to push back, so the skin between them pushes a lot of water. Then she folds her toes to bring the foot forward. Frogs kick with long, webbed back legs.
examples: A rohu fish swings her tail from side to side.
Ducks paddle in the backwaters of Kuttanad in Kerala.
A frog in a pond kicks both back legs at once.
explanations.art: A duck under the water seen from below, one foot spread open pushing back and the other foot folded, coming forward.

explanations.context: This card is about snakes, earthworms and snails, who move without legs.
explanations.definition: Animals without legs move by pushing parts of their body against the ground and the things on it.
explanations.description: A snake bends her body into curves. Each curve pushes sideways against stones, sticks and bumps, and that pushes the snake forward. On very smooth glass she has little to push on, so she slides about and moves slowly. An earthworm makes her body long and thin, then short and fat, and tiny bristles grip the soil. A snail glides on a layer of slime.
examples: A rat snake moves fast through grass, pushing on the stems.
An earthworm stretches forward, grips, and pulls the back part along.
A snail leaves a shiny trail of slime on a wall after rain.
explanations.art: A snake from above in an S-shape, with small arrows where the curves push against stones.

explanations.context: This card is about the different kinds of teeth, and how they match what an animal eats.
explanations.definition: Animals have teeth shaped for their food: incisors cut, canines grip and tear, and molars grind.
explanations.description: A cow eats grass. She has no top front teeth, only a hard pad of gum, and she tears grass off between that pad and her bottom front teeth. Her wide, flat molars grind the grass as her jaw moves from side to side. A tiger's long canines grip and tear meat, her back teeth cut like scissors, and her jaw moves mostly up and down. A squirrel's front teeth never stop growing, so gnawing keeps them short. Humans eat many kinds of food, so we have all three kinds of teeth.
examples: A child has 20 milk teeth. Most grown-ups have 32 teeth.
An elephant's tusks are two very long front teeth.
A snake swallows a frog whole, and her jaws stretch very wide.
explanations.art: Three open mouths side by side: a cow's with flat back teeth and no top front teeth, a tiger's with long canines, and a child's with all three kinds.

explanations.context: This card is about how a bird's beak matches the food that bird eats.
explanations.definition: Birds have no teeth. Each bird's beak is shaped for the way that bird gets food.
explanations.description: A sparrow's beak is short and thick, strong enough to crack open seeds. A parrot's hooked beak cracks nuts and also helps the parrot climb. A kingfisher's beak is long, straight and sharp, for grabbing fish. A black kite's hooked beak tears meat. A duck's flat beak has tiny comb-like edges that let water out and keep food in. A crow's beak is a strong, middle-sized beak that suits almost any food, and crows eat almost anything.
examples: A white-throated kingfisher sits on a wire above a paddy field, watching for fish and frogs.
A rose-ringed parrot holds a chilli in one foot and bites the chilli with her hooked beak.
A house sparrow cracks rice grains with her short, thick beak.
explanations.art: Six bird heads in a row: sparrow, parrot, kingfisher, black kite, duck and crow, each with a small picture of their food.

explanations.concept: One bone plan in many limbs
explanations.context: This card is about the bones inside the legs, wings and flippers of many animals. They turn out to be the same bones.
explanations.definition: The arm of a human, the wing of a bat and a bird, the front leg of a frog and the flipper of a whale are built from the same set of bones.
explanations.description: Each one has one long upper bone, then two bones side by side, then a group of small wrist bones, then fingers or toes. In a bat the finger bones are very long, to hold the skin of the wing. In a whale they are wrapped inside a stiff flipper. This is because all these animals come from the same long-ago ancestors: fish with bony, fleshy fins.
examples: Feel your own arm: one bone above the elbow, two below it.
Most of a bat's wing is a hand with very long fingers.
A frog's front leg has the same bones as your arm, only shorter.
explanations.art: Four limbs side by side, with the same bones coloured the same: a human arm, a bat wing, a frog's front leg and a whale's flipper.

explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: how the first birds began to fly.
explanations.description: Birds come from small dinosaurs with feathers. But nobody saw the first flights, so scientists argue about how flying began.
examples: Some small feathered dinosaurs had feathers on all four limbs.
Young chukar partridges flap their small wings to help them run up steep slopes.

perspectives.explanation: Small feathered animals climbed trees and glided down, like the flying lizard. Over a very long time, gliding turned into flapping.
Small feathered animals ran fast on the ground and flapped to leap higher, to run up slopes or to catch insects. Over time, the flaps lifted them off the ground.
Maybe both happened, in different animals. The evidence is a few rare fossils, so the question is still open.

explanations.art: Two small feathered dinosaurs: one gliding down from a tree, one running and flapping up a slope.

agreed.text: To move, an animal must push on something: the ground, the water or the air.
agreed.evidence: On ice or a very slippery floor, feet slide back and a walker hardly moves. Slow-motion films show wings pushing air down and fish tails pushing water back.

agreed.text: Teeth and beaks are shaped for the food an animal eats.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can often tell what an animal ate from the shape of their teeth, even in fossils. Plant-eaters have wide grinding teeth. Meat-eaters have sharp tearing teeth.

agreed.text: The limbs of birds, bats, frogs, whales and humans are built from the same set of bones.
agreed.evidence: When scientists compare the skeletons, they find the same pattern of bones in each limb: one bone, then two bones, then small wrist bones, then fingers or toes.

challenging.for: Snakes look shiny, and some animals without legs, like earthworms and snails, are slimy.
challenging.against: A snake's skin is dry and covered in scales. Earthworms and snails are slimy, but snakes are not.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many people make about snakes.

challenging.claim: Animals with big, sharp teeth eat only meat.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Tigers and leopards have big canines and eat only meat.
challenging.against: The sloth bear of India has big canines, but eats mostly termites, ants and fruit. Monkeys and fruit bats have pointed canines and eat lots of fruit.
challenging.context: This card is about whether teeth always tell you an animal's food.

challenging.claim: Birds take off using only their wings.
challenging.who: What many people think when they watch a bird fly
challenging.for: Wings do the flying once a bird is in the air.
challenging.against: Scientists filmed birds taking off and measured the push of their feet. Many birds get most of their starting speed from a jump with their legs, then the wings take over.
challenging.context: This card is about how a bird leaves the ground.

challenging.for: A big kangaroo or a horse can jump a long way.
challenging.against: A tiny flea or grasshopper jumps many times the length of their own body. An elephant cannot jump at all. Size alone does not decide how far an animal jumps.
challenging.context: This card is about size and jumping.

big_questions.q: In the Jump Test, your legs were bent and still just before each jump. Was the jump already in your legs, waiting?
big_questions.hint: Think about what your legs did in the small moment before your feet left the floor.

big_questions.q: Your arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper have the same bones. Are they three different things, or one thing in three shapes?
big_questions.hint: Feel the bones of your arm. Then look at a picture of a bat's wing.

big_questions.q: A frog decides when to jump. What does a frog notice before she jumps?
big_questions.hint: Watch how still a frog or a cat sits before a jump. What might they be watching for?

big_questions.q: Every animal moves by pushing on the ground, the water or the air. Could anything move in a place with nothing to push on?
big_questions.hint: Think about a person floating in space. What could they push on?

big_questions.q: Humans can walk, run, jump, swim and climb, but cannot fly. Is it better to do many things a little, or one thing very well?
big_questions.hint: Compare a crow, who eats almost anything, with a kingfisher, who is very good at catching fish.

story.title: The Frog on the Bathroom Wall
story.note: A made-up story. The common Indian tree frog really does come into bathrooms in Kerala in the monsoon, climbs tiles with sticky toe pads, and has long back legs that fold up when she sits.
text: It rained all night in Kochi. In the morning, Anjali went into the bathroom to brush her teeth, and stopped.
A small brown frog was sitting on the white wall tiles, just above the water bucket. She had dark stripes on her back and big gold eyes.
"Ammamma!" Anjali called softly. "There is a frog on the wall!"

Anjali was seven. She lived on the first floor of a building near the backwaters, with Amma, her grandmother Ammamma, and her brother Joel, who was five. Ammamma had taught biology in a school for thirty years.
Joel came running first. "Catch her!" he shouted, and reached out his hand.
"Wait," said Ammamma, from the door. "Don't grab her. A frog's skin is thin and soft. She drinks water through her skin, and soap or dry hands can hurt her."
Joel pulled his hand back. They all looked at the frog. The frog looked at them, and did not move.
"How is she holding on to the wall?" asked Anjali. "The tiles are so smooth."

"Look at her toes," said Ammamma. "See the little round pads at the ends? They are sticky and soft. They press close to the tile, and wet tiles help them hold. This is a tree frog. Tree frogs climb trees, and walls too."
Anjali leaned closer. The frog's front legs were short and thin. Her back legs were folded up tight under her body, so she looked like a small brown ball.
"Her back legs are so short," said Anjali.
Ammamma smiled. "Are they? Keep watching."
Joel could not keep still. He took a step forward, and his slipper squeaked on the floor.
The frog jumped.

For one moment, Anjali saw her back legs open out. They opened like a folding ruler, in three parts. They were long, longer than the frog's whole head and body together. Then, plop, the frog was in the water bucket.
"Where did those long legs come from?" Anjali gasped.
"They were there all the time," said Ammamma. "Folded up, ready. A frog sits with her legs bent, so that she can push off fast."

In the bucket, the frog kicked both back legs at once. Her toes spread wide as she pushed back, and Anjali saw thin skin stretched between them, like a little fan. The frog shot across the water to the other side.
"Her feet are like a duck's!" said Joel.
"Yes," said Ammamma. "Webbed feet. The skin between the toes pushes a lot of water back, so she moves fast. When her legs come forward again, she pulls her toes together."
"Can we keep her?" asked Joel.
Ammamma shook her head. "She is a wild frog. She needs to eat insects and live outside, near the rain. We will take her to the plants by the gate."
Ammamma held a mug in the water, and the frog swam into the mug. Anjali put a piece of cardboard over the top, gently. They walked down the stairs together.

Near the gate, under the big banana plant, there was a puddle from the night's rain. Ammamma tipped the mug. The frog sat for a moment on the wet ground. Then she folded her legs, waited, and jumped into the leaves.
Back upstairs, Anjali could not stop thinking about the jump.
"Joel," she said, "jump like a frog."
Joel stood stiff and straight, and tried to jump without bending his knees. He hardly went anywhere. He wobbled and laughed.
"No," said Anjali. "Watch me." She crouched down low, with her knees bent, like the frog on the wall. She waited. Then she pushed hard with both legs and flew forward across the corridor.
"You went far!" said Joel. He crouched too, and this time he jumped much farther.
"So the jump starts before the jump," said Anjali slowly. "It starts when your legs are folded up."

Ammamma was listening from the kitchen. "The cat downstairs crouches before she jumps on the wall," she said. "The grasshopper on the money plant has huge back legs, folded up like the frog's. Even a pigeon bends her legs and jumps a little before she flies."
That night it rained again. From the plants by the gate came a loud tok, tok, tok. The frogs were calling to each other in the dark.

Anjali opened her notebook. She drew the frog twice: once folded up small on the wall, and once in the air with her long legs stretched out behind. Then, next to the frog, she drew herself, crouching at the start line, ready to jump.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Anjali sees that the frog's long back legs were there all the time, folded up. A jump begins with bent legs, and a longer push gives a longer jump. She tries it with her own body, and finds that she and the frog jump in the same way.
ask: Why did the frog look as if she had short back legs, when she was sitting on the wall?
Why did Joel hardly move when he jumped with straight legs?
How did the frog's webbed feet help her swim across the bucket?
Why did Ammamma say they could not keep the frog?

printables.title: A track of 13 squares to draw on paper

rules: Before you play, draw each animal on that animal's card, so that a child who cannot read yet can play.
Lay the 8 animal cards face up in a row. Put a coin on Start as the message.
Mix the 12 place cards and put them face down in a pile.
Turn over the top place card and read the place aloud, but do not read the back.
The team chooses one animal who can get through that place, and says how: with legs, wings, fins, sticky toes or the whole body. If the team is stuck, read the back aloud and choose from it.
Check the back. If your animal is named there, move the message one square forward. If not, nothing moves, and you choose again.
Each animal can carry the message only twice. When an animal has gone twice, turn that card face down to rest.

If every animal who can get through is resting, turn all 8 animal cards face up again. You can do this only once in a game. If it happens again, put the place card aside, and the message stays where it is.
The game ends when all 12 place cards are used. The team wins if the message is at Home. If not, count how many squares the message moved, and play again to beat that number.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and draw the animals together. 2. Draw the track. 3. Lay out the animal cards and put the coin on Start.
flow.say: We have to get a message all the way home. These animals will carry it for us.
flow.kid: Draw the animals. Put the coin on Start.

flow.do: 1. Turn over a place card. 2. Your child chooses an animal and says how that animal gets through. 3. Check the back and move the message.
flow.say: A tiny crack in the wall! Who can get through? How?
flow.kid: Who can get through? How do they move?

ask.q: Why can the crow cross the wide river, but not the narrow pipe?
good: The crow can fly over the river.
The crow is too big for the pipe, and her wings don't fit.

flow.parent: Let your child plan ahead. Only the ant and the gecko can go along the ceiling, so they should be saved for that card.

flow.do: When the game ends, ask the check question.
flow.say: Which animal could get through the most places? Which could get through the fewest?
flow.kid: Who could go to the most places?

check.q: Which animal could go only where there is water?
check.why: A fish breathes with gills and swims with fins, so the rohu fish must stay in water. The duck and the snake can move on land and in water. Each body suits some places and not others.

printables.title: A score sheet with three rows of points and one column for each player

rules: Mix the clue cards and put them face down in a pile.
The reader takes the top card and reads clue 1 aloud.
The other players may guess. A right guess after clue 1 wins 3 points.
If nobody is right, read clue 2. A right guess now wins 2 points. After clue 3, a right guess wins 1 point. If nobody is right after clue 3, nobody scores.
Each player gets one guess for each clue.
After each card, the reader turns it over and reads the answer aloud. Then the next player becomes the reader.
When all 12 cards are done, the player with the most points wins. With 2 players, you take turns as reader and guesser. A grown-up can read for a child who cannot read yet.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and draw the score sheet.
flow.say: I will read clues about an animal's mouth. Guess the animal as early as you can.
flow.kid: Listen to the clues. Guess the animal!

flow.do: 1. Take turns being the reader. 2. Read one clue at a time. 3. Score the guesses.
flow.say: Clue one: I have a beak and no teeth. Who am I?
flow.kid: Listen to each clue and guess. An early guess gets more points.

ask.q: How did the shape of the mouth help you guess?
good: A hooked beak means tearing meat or cracking nuts.
Long pointed teeth mean a meat-eater.

flow.parent: Every first clue says beak or teeth. That alone is not enough to guess, so the second clue matters most.

flow.do: Add up the points, then ask the check question.
flow.say: Who has the most points? Now, one more puzzle.
flow.kid: Add up your points!

check.q: A bird has a long, straight, sharp beak and sits by water. What does the bird most likely eat?
check.why: A long, straight, sharp beak is good for grabbing slippery fish, like a kingfisher's. Seed-eaters have short, thick beaks. Nectar-drinkers have long, thin, curved beaks.

experiments.title: The Jump Test: do bent knees make you jump farther?
experiments.context: In this experiment your child jumps forward from a start line three ways: with straight legs, with a small bend in the knees, and with a big bend. You mark and measure each jump to find out how bending the legs changes a jump.
experiments.question: Does bending your knees before a jump make you jump farther? And does a bigger bend make a longer jump?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which jump will go farthest: straight legs, a small bend, or a big bend? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same child jumps every time, from the same start line, with both feet together and hands on hips. Hands on hips stop the arms from helping, so only the knee bend changes. We try each way three times, because one jump can be lucky or unlucky, and we keep the longest.

materials.item: a clear stretch of floor about 2 metres long, in a hall or corridor, not slippery
a dupatta, a long scarf or a strip of tape, for the start line
small markers such as coins or bottle caps
a measuring tape or a 30 cm ruler, or a grown-up's foot to measure in foot-lengths
paper and a pencil for the results table

experiments.safety: Jump barefoot on a dry floor, or on a dhurrie or mat that does not slide. Socks on tiles are slippery. Move chairs and tables out of the way, and land with soft, bent knees.

schedule.what: Jump three ways from a start line: straight legs, a small bend and a big bend. Mark and measure each jump.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw a stick picture of yourself just before your longest jump.

flow.do: 1. Clear about 2 metres of floor. 2. Lay the dupatta straight across the floor as the start line. 3. Your child stands with toes just behind the line, feet together, hands on hips.
flow.say: This is our jumping track. Every jump starts with your toes behind the dupatta and your hands on your hips.
flow.kid: Stand with your toes behind the line. Put your hands on your hips.

flow.do: Show the three ways to jump: with straight legs, with a small bend, and with a big bend like sitting on a low stool. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Which jump do you think will go farthest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which jump will go farthest? Straight, small bend or big bend? Why?

good: The big bend, because a frog crouches low.
Straight legs, because my legs are longer when they are straight.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write it down exactly as your child says it. Do not explain anything yet. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. Your child keeps the knees straight and stiff, and jumps forward using only ankles and toes. 2. Put a coin at the back of the heel that lands nearest the start line. 3. Measure from the line to the coin. 4. Do it three times.
flow.say: Straight legs first. Keep your knees stiff, like sticks. Now jump as far as you can.
flow.kid: Keep your knees stiff. Jump forward as far as you can.
flow.parent: Measure from the start line to the back of the heel that landed nearest the line. With stiff knees most children only hop a short way.

flow.do: 1. Now your child bends the knees a little, then jumps. 2. Mark and measure each landing. 3. Do it three times and write each one down.
flow.say: Now bend your knees just a little bit, then jump. Hands stay on your hips.
flow.kid: Bend your knees a little. Then jump!

flow.do: 1. Now your child bends the knees a lot, as if sitting on a low stool, then jumps. 2. Mark and measure each landing. 3. Do it three times.
flow.say: Now the big bend. Bend down low, as if you are sitting on a small stool. Then push off hard.
flow.kid: Bend down low, like a frog. Then push hard!
flow.parent: Do not let your child squat all the way down to the floor. A bend about as low as a small stool is enough. If they wobble, let them rest and try again.

flow.do: Circle the longest jump for each way. Put the three longest jumps in order, from shortest to longest.
flow.say: Let's find your longest jump for each way. Which way won?
flow.kid: Circle your longest jumps. Which way went farthest?

options: A big bend, like sitting on a low stool
check.why: With stiff legs, your feet can push for only a tiny moment. A big bend lets your legs push on the floor for longer as they straighten. A longer push sends you off faster, so you go farther. If your small bend won, that is a real result too. Write it down.

flow.do: Ask your child what they think now, what they saw, and why. Then tell them about the frog's folded legs.
flow.say: So, what did you find out? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: What did you find? Why did bending help?

ask.q: Why did the big bend make you jump farther?
good: My legs pushed on the floor for longer.
When my legs straightened, they pushed me hard.
Straight legs had nothing left to straighten.

flow.parent: A strong answer says what happened (claim), gives the numbers (evidence), and says why: the legs push only while they are straightening, so a bigger bend means a longer push. Then tell your child that a frog's long back legs fold up in a Z, so the frog gets a very long push.

experiments.title: Press or Grind: how does a cow chew grass?
experiments.context: In this experiment your child crushes leaves between a steel plate and the flat bottom of a steel tumbler, in two ways: pressing straight down, and rubbing round and round. This shows why a cow's jaw moves from side to side when she chews grass.
experiments.question: Which way breaks a leaf into small bits: pressing straight down, or rubbing round and round?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will pressing down hard or rubbing round and round break the leaf up more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same kind of leaf, the same tumbler and the same plate. We move the tumbler 10 times each way, and press about as hard each time. Only the way of moving changes. We try each way with two leaves, because one leaf can be tougher than another.
results_table: What the leaf looked like after 10 moves
Any green juice on the plate?

materials.item: fresh leaves, such as curry leaves, coriander, spinach or a few blades of grass
a steel plate
a steel tumbler or a small steel katori with a flat bottom
a small piece of roti, dosa or bread to chew

schedule.what: Press two leaves and rub two leaves with the bottom of a steel tumbler. Compare them. Then chew and feel how your own jaw moves.

experiments.record: Stick or draw one pressed leaf and one rubbed leaf side by side, and write which way made smaller bits.

flow.do: 1. Put two leaves at one side of the plate and two at the other. 2. Show the two ways to crush a leaf with the bottom of the tumbler: press straight down and lift, or press and rub round and round.
flow.say: The tumbler is our tooth, and the plate is another tooth. We can crush the leaf two ways.
flow.kid: The tumbler is a tooth. The plate is a tooth too.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Which way will break the leaf into smaller bits, pressing or rubbing? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pressing or rubbing: which breaks the leaf more? Why?

flow.do: 1. Your child presses the tumbler straight down on one leaf and lifts it, 10 times. 2. Do the same on the second leaf. 3. Look closely at both.
flow.say: Press straight down and lift. Count to ten. Press hard, like squeezing a lime.
flow.kid: Press down and lift. Do it ten times. Look at the leaf.
flow.parent: Pressed leaves usually go flat and get dark, bruised marks, and may leave a little juice, but they mostly stay in one piece. Leaves differ: curry leaves are tough and spinach is soft. If the result is not clear, count the bits.

flow.do: 1. Now your child presses the tumbler on a new leaf and rubs it round and round and side to side, 10 times. 2. Do the same on the last leaf. 3. Compare all four.
flow.say: Now press and rub round and round. Count to ten. What happens to this leaf?
flow.kid: Press and rub round and round, ten times. What happens?

ask.q: What do the rubbed leaves look like?
good: They are torn into little bits.
There is green juice on the plate.
They are mushy.

flow.parent: Rubbed leaves tear into shreds and leave a green smear on the plate. Rubbing breaks the leaf because the tumbler and the plate slide past each other. That tears the leaf instead of only squeezing it.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts two fingers on each cheek, just in front of the ears. 2. Then they chew a piece of roti slowly. 3. Ask how the jaw moves.
flow.say: Put your fingers here, in front of your ears. Now chew slowly. Does your jaw only go up and down?
flow.kid: Fingers on your cheeks. Chew slowly. How does your jaw move?

ask.q: How does your jaw move when you chew?
good: Up and down, and a little bit side to side.
It goes round a bit.

flow.parent: People's jaws move up and down and also a little from side to side, so our back teeth can grind. A cow's jaw swings far from side to side, and her wide molars rub the grass into a mush. A tiger's jaw moves mostly up and down, and her back teeth cut meat like scissors.

flow.do: Ask what your child thinks now, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Which way broke the leaf more? So why does a cow move her jaw from side to side?
flow.kid: Which way broke the leaf? Why does a cow chew side to side?

check.q: A cow eats grass all day. Why does her jaw move from side to side?
options: So her flat back teeth rub the grass into tiny bits
Because her front teeth are too big
check.why: In the test, rubbing tore the leaf into bits, but pressing only flattened it. A cow's wide molars rub past each other as her jaw swings sideways, grinding tough grass into a mush she can swallow.

activities.title: Ready, Steady, Crouch: how jumpers get ready
activities.context: In this short activity your child moves like three animals who jump: a frog, a cat and a grasshopper. They notice what every jumper does just before the jump.

materials.item: a clear space on the floor, or a mat

schedule.what: Be a frog, a cat and a grasshopper getting ready to jump. Notice what each one does first.

activities.record: Draw one animal just before a jump.

flow.do: 1. Call out a frog, a cat and a grasshopper, one at a time. 2. Your child shows how that animal gets ready to jump. 3. Then they make one small, soft jump.
flow.say: Be a frog on a wet path. Get ready to jump. Now be a cat who wants to jump onto a wall.
flow.kid: Be a frog. Get ready to jump! Now be a cat.
flow.parent: A frog sits low with legs folded. A cat crouches, wiggles a little and stares at the wall. A grasshopper's big back legs are folded high, like a bent letter V.

flow.do: Ask what all three did before jumping.
flow.say: What did the frog, the cat and the grasshopper all do just before jumping?
flow.kid: What did every jumper do first?

ask.q: What did every jumper do before the jump?
good: They all bent their legs.
They crouched down low first.
They kept still and looked.

check.q: What does a cat do just before she jumps onto a wall?
options: She stands up tall on straight legs
She crouches low with her legs bent
check.why: Jumpers bend their legs first. Bent legs can straighten fast and push on the ground for longer. The Jump Test checks if this is true for you too.

activities.title: Wing Push: flap a notebook like a wing
activities.context: In this activity your child swings a big notebook down flat, like a bird's wing, and then edge first, like a knife. They watch what happens to small bits of tissue on the floor, and feel the air push back.

materials.item: a big notebook, a file or a piece of cardboard about the size of a notebook
a tissue or a piece of newspaper, torn into 10 small bits

schedule.what: Flap a notebook flat and then edge first above tissue bits. See which way blows them away, and feel the push.

activities.record: Draw a bird with wings spread wide, pushing air down, and arrows showing the air.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan and close the window. 2. Put the tissue bits in a small pile on the floor. 3. Your child holds the notebook flat, about one hand-width above the bits. 4. Swing the notebook down fast, without touching the bits.
flow.say: Your notebook is a wing. Hold it flat and swing it down fast. Don't touch the tissue. What happens?
flow.kid: Hold the notebook flat. Swing it down fast. Watch the tissue!

ask.q: What happened to the tissue bits?
good: They blew away.
They flew everywhere.
The air pushed them.

flow.do: 1. Pile up the bits again. 2. Now your child holds the notebook edge first, like a knife, and swings it down the same way.
flow.say: Now hold it on its edge, like a knife. Swing it down the same way. What happens now?
flow.kid: Now hold it on its edge. Swing it down. What happens?
flow.parent: Edge first, the notebook slices through the air and hardly moves the tissue. Flat, the notebook pushes a lot of air down. It is also harder to swing flat, because the air pushes back on the notebook.

flow.do: Ask which way was harder to swing, and talk about how a bird uses the wing.
flow.say: Which way was harder to swing? A bird spreads her wings wide and flat to push down. Why?
flow.kid: Which way was harder? Why does a bird spread her wings wide?

check.q: Why does a bird spread her wings wide and flat when she flaps down?
options: To push a lot of air down, so the air pushes her up
check.why: A wide, flat wing pushes a lot of air down, like your flat notebook. The air pushes back up on the wing, and that holds the bird up. On the way up, many birds bend their wings in a little, like turning the notebook on its edge.

activities.title: Snake Wiggle: move with no legs
activities.context: In this activity your child lies on their tummy, keeps arms and legs still, and tries to move forward like a snake. They try first on a bare floor, then with cushions to push against.

materials.item: a clear, clean floor about 2 metres long
cushions, pillows, school bags or rolled-up bedsheets

schedule.what: Try to slide forward like a snake on a bare floor, then with cushions to push against.

activities.record: Draw a snake from above, in an S shape, with stones beside the curves.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies on their tummy on the bare floor. 2. Arms stay by the sides, and feet do not push. 3. They try to move forward by wiggling for one minute.
flow.say: You are a snake. No arms and no feet. Can you move forward just by wiggling?
flow.kid: Lie on your tummy. Keep arms and feet still. Wiggle forward!
flow.parent: On a smooth floor your child will twist about a lot and move very little. That is what this step is meant to show. Keep it playful.

flow.do: 1. Put cushions in two zigzag rows along the path, a little apart. 2. Your child tries again, pushing the sides of the body against the cushions.
flow.say: These cushions are the stones on a snake's path. Push your sides against them as you wiggle.
flow.kid: Push your sides on the cushions. Can you move now?

ask.q: Was it easier with the cushions? Why?
good: Yes, because I could push on them.
The cushions gave me something to push against.

flow.parent: Cushions are softer than stones, so your child may still move only a little. Stack the cushions against a wall or use rolled-up mats to give a firmer push.

flow.do: Talk about how real snakes and earthworms move.
flow.say: A snake pushes the curves of her body against stones, sticks and bumps. What would happen to a snake on smooth glass?
flow.kid: How does a snake push? What about on smooth glass?

check.q: How does a snake move forward without legs?
options: She pushes the curves of her body against bumps on the ground
check.why: A snake bends into curves and pushes each curve sideways against stones, sticks and bumps. The ground pushes back and moves her forward. On smooth glass she has little to push on, so she slides about.

flow.parent: An earthworm makes her body long and thin, then short and fat, one part at a time. Tiny bristles on her body grip the soil.

activities.title: My Teeth Map: count, draw and bite
activities.context: In this activity your child counts their own teeth in a mirror, finds any gaps where milk teeth have fallen out, and draws a map of their teeth. Then they bite a slice of cucumber to see the marks their front teeth leave.

materials.item: a mirror
a slice of cucumber or apple, about as thick as a finger
paper and a pencil
blue, yellow and green pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Count your teeth in a mirror and draw a teeth map. Bite a cucumber slice and look at the marks.

activities.record: Your teeth map, with cutting, pointed and grinding teeth coloured in three colours.

flow.do: 1. At the mirror, your child counts the top teeth, then the bottom teeth. 2. Count gaps and new big teeth too. 3. Draw a top row and a bottom row of little boxes, one box for each tooth.
flow.say: Let's count your top teeth first, from one side to the other. Now the bottom ones.
flow.kid: Count your top teeth. Now count your bottom teeth.
flow.parent: A child has 20 milk teeth. Between about 6 and 12 years of age, these fall out one by one and bigger teeth grow in. A seven-year-old often has gaps at the front, and some new big front teeth or new back molars.

flow.do: Colour the map: front cutting teeth blue, pointed teeth yellow, back grinding teeth green.
flow.say: The flat front ones are cutting teeth. The pointed ones are canines. The wide back ones are molars.
flow.kid: Colour cutting teeth blue, pointed ones yellow, back ones green.

flow.do: 1. Your child bites into the cucumber slice with only the front teeth. 2. Look at the marks together. 3. Compare your child's bite with a cow's: a cow has no top front teeth.
flow.say: Bite with just your front teeth. What shape are the marks?
flow.kid: Bite with your front teeth. Look at the marks!

ask.q: What shape did your front teeth leave?
good: A curved row of flat cuts.
Straight lines, like a knife.
A gap where my tooth fell out.

check.q: A cow has no top front teeth. What does she have instead?
check.why: A cow has a hard pad of gum at the front of the top jaw. She holds grass between that pad and her bottom front teeth, tears it off, and grinds it with her molars.

setup.caption: 2. Draw and colour your teeth map.

activities.title: Take-off Watch (if birds land near your window)
activities.context: In this activity you and your child watch a pigeon, crow or myna on a ledge or wire near your window, and look closely at how the bird takes off. Do this only if birds often come near your window.

materials.item: a window where pigeons, crows or mynas often sit
a phone camera with slow-motion video, if you have one

schedule.what: Watch a bird on a ledge or wire. See if the bird bends the legs and jumps before flying.

activities.record: Draw the bird in two pictures: just before take-off, and just after.

flow.do: 1. Sit quietly at the window. 2. When a bird is about to fly, watch the legs. 3. If you can, film the take-off in slow motion and watch it again.
flow.say: Watch the bird's legs, not the wings. What do the legs do when the bird takes off?
flow.kid: Watch the bird's legs. What happens when the bird flies?
flow.parent: Many birds bend their legs and push off with a jump, then start flapping. Pigeons often clap their wings as they leave. If no bird comes, try another day.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw.
flow.say: Did the bird jump first, or flap first? How is that like the Jump Test, where you bent your knees before jumping?
flow.kid: Did the bird jump first, or flap first?

ask.q: What did the bird do first?
good: The bird bent the legs and jumped.
The bird crouched and then flapped.

projects.title: My Movers and Eaters Diary
projects.context: In this three-day project your child watches one real animal each day. They draw how that animal moves, what the animal pushes on, and what the animal's mouth looks like.

materials.item: 3 sheets of paper folded and stapled into a small book
pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Watch ants on the floor or wall. Draw how they move and what their mouths do with food.
Watch a bird at the window or on a wire. Draw how the bird moves and the shape of the beak.
Watch yourself or someone at home walk, jump and eat. Draw your legs and your teeth.

projects.record: The finished diary, with three animals: how each moves, what each pushes on, and the shape of each mouth.

flow.do: 1. Put a few grains of sugar where you have seen ants, and wait. 2. Your child watches an ant walk and carry food. 3. Draw the ant, with six legs, and write what the ant pushes on.
flow.say: What does the ant push on to walk? What does she do with the sugar?
flow.kid: Watch an ant walk. Draw her legs. What does she push on?
flow.parent: Ants have six legs and strong jaws that work from side to side, like pincers. They carry food in their jaws. If no ants come, try again the next day.

flow.do: Your child watches a crow, pigeon or myna and draws the bird's beak and how the bird moves: walking, hopping or flying.
flow.say: Does this bird walk or hop? What shape is the beak? What food might that beak be good for?
flow.kid: Does the bird walk or hop? Draw the beak.

flow.do: Your child draws themselves walking and jumping, and draws their teeth. Then compare all three pages.
flow.say: Now you are the animal. What do you push on? What kinds of teeth do you have?
flow.kid: Draw yourself jumping. Draw your teeth.

check.q: What do an ant, a crow and you all push on to walk?
check.why: Walkers push back on the ground with their feet or legs. The ground pushes back, and they move forward. A crow also pushes on the air when she flies.

challenges.title: Make a Flying Lizard: the slowest paper glider
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. The flying lizard of the Western Ghats glides between trees on flaps of skin. You make a paper lizard that falls as slowly as possible from the same height.
challenges.problem: Can you make a paper lizard that takes the longest time to reach the floor, when dropped from the same height?
constraints: Use one sheet of paper, no bigger than a notebook page, and one paper clip as the lizard's head.
Hold each paper lizard flat and drop each one from the same height, such as your shoulder.
materials: a phone stopwatch to time the fall, or count out loud
general: Make the paper lizard wide and flat, like the lizard's spread-out skin flaps.
Put the paper clip at the front as a head, so the lizard falls nose first and goes forward.
Fold the side edges up a little to keep the lizard steady.
creative: Cut the wings into a long, wavy ribbon shape, like a flying snake.
Try a small tail at the back, and see if the lizard flies straighter.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own slowest glider. Then tell someone at home why your shape falls slowly.

flow.do: Read the challenge. First crumple one sheet into a ball and drop it, to see a fast fall.
flow.say: A paper ball falls fast. Can you make a paper lizard that falls very slowly?
flow.kid: Drop a paper ball. Now make a slow paper lizard!

flow.do: Your child makes a paper lizard, drops the paper lizard from shoulder height and counts how long the fall takes. Then they change the shape and try again.
flow.say: How long did that take? What could you change to make the fall slower?
flow.kid: Drop your lizard. Count. Change the shape. Try again.
flow.parent: A wide, flat shape falls slowly. A paper clip at the front stops it from tumbling, but its weight can also make the fall faster, so try with and without the clip. A grown-up helps with scissors.

flow.do: Test the best design three times and talk about why it works.
flow.say: Why does your best lizard fall so slowly?
flow.kid: Why does your lizard fall slowly?

ask.q: Why did your best lizard fall slowly?
good: It is wide and flat, so it pushes on a lot of air.

check.q: Why does the flying lizard spread out the skin flaps on the sides?
options: To make a wide, flat shape that pushes on a lot of air and falls slowly
check.why: A wide, flat shape pushes on a lot of air as the lizard falls. The air pushes back and slows the fall, so the lizard glides forward to the next tree. Your flat paper lizard fell slower than the paper ball for the same reason.

items.p: Sort each animal by the main way they move.
items.why: A cat walks on four legs. A flying crow and a butterfly use wings. A fish swims with fins. An earthworm and a snake have no legs and move with the whole body.
items.art: Six small drawings: a cat, a flying crow, a fish, an earthworm, a butterfly and a snake.

items.p: Draw a line from each beak to the food it is best for.
items.why: Short, thick beaks crack seeds. Long, sharp beaks grab fish. Long, curved beaks reach nectar deep in flowers. Hooked beaks tear meat.
items.art: Four bird heads on the left and four foods on the right, mixed up.

items.p: How many legs do one duck, one frog and one ant have altogether?
items.why: A duck has 2 legs, a frog has 4 and an ant has 6. 2 and 4 make 6, and 6 more makes 12.
items.art: A duck, a frog and an ant standing in a row.

items.p: Which body part pushes on the water when a rohu fish swims forward?
items.why: A fish bends her body from side to side, and the tail fin pushes water back. That pushes the fish forward. The other fins steer and keep her steady.

items.p: Birds have teeth inside their beaks.
items.why: False. Birds alive today have no teeth. Their beaks are shaped to crack, grab, tear, sip or strain their food.

items.p: Pick a food: seeds, fish or nectar. Draw the head of a bird with a beak that fits that food.
items.a: A bird head with a short, thick beak for seeds, a long, straight, sharp beak for fish, or a long, thin, curved beak for nectar.
items.why: A strong drawing gives the beak a shape that suits the chosen food, because each beak is shaped for the way that bird gets food.
items.art: An empty box with the words seeds, fish and nectar along the bottom.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the Jump Test, why did you hardly move with straight legs?
items.a: My legs were already straight, so they could not straighten any more and could not push on the floor for long.
items.why: A strong answer says that legs push only while they straighten, and straight legs have no bend left to straighten.

items.p: Label the teeth in this mouth: cutting teeth, pointed teeth, grinding teeth.
a: cutting teeth: the flat ones at the very front
pointed teeth: one on each side of the front teeth
grinding teeth: the wide ones at the back
items.why: Incisors at the front cut. Canines beside them grip and tear. Molars at the back grind food into small bits.
items.art: A drawing of a child's open mouth with three empty label lines pointing to the front, the side and the back teeth.

items.p: Three of these animals have wings. Which one does not?
items.why: A frog has no wings. A bat has skin wings, a housefly has two thin wings, and a pigeon has feathered wings.

items.p: A place where two bones meet, so the body can bend, is called a ________.
items.why: Your knee, elbow and ankle are joints. A frog's long back legs bend at three joints, so they fold up small.

items.p: Put the steps of a frog's jump in order.
items: The frog sits with her back legs folded up.
Her back legs straighten fast and push on the ground.
She flies through the air with her legs stretched out.
She lands on her front legs.
items.why: A jump starts with bent legs. The push happens while the legs straighten, and only then does the frog leave the ground.

items.p: Meenakshi and her friend Farhan live in Madurai. They are looking at pictures of a cow's teeth and a tiger's teeth.

views.says: The tiger's teeth are better. They are long and sharp, and they can tear anything.
The cow's teeth are better. A cow can eat grass all day, and grass is everywhere.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says what the other side gets right. For example: the tiger's teeth are best for meat, but they could not grind grass. The cow's teeth are best for grass, but they could not catch and tear meat.
items.why: Each set of teeth is very good at one kind of food. Which is better depends on what the animal eats. A strong answer uses the shape of the teeth as evidence.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: in the Press or Grind test, which way broke the leaf into small bits? Say why that helps a cow.
items.a: Rubbing round and round tore the leaf into bits and made green juice. Pressing only flattened it. A cow rubs her flat back teeth from side to side, so the grass is ground up small.
items.why: A strong answer gives the result of the test (rubbing tore the leaf) and links it to the side-to-side chewing of a cow.

items.p: Two frogs are the same size. One has short back legs and one has long back legs. Which frog most likely jumps farther?
opts: The frog with short back legs
The frog with long back legs
items.why: Long legs that fold up can push on the ground for longer as they straighten. A longer push gives a faster start and a longer jump. That is what your bent knees showed in the Jump Test.

items.p: Sort these animals by what they eat.
items.why: Cows and elephants eat plants. Tigers and kingfishers eat other animals. Crows and most humans eat both plants and animals.

items.p: Label the duck's foot: toes, web of skin. Then write which way the foot pushes the water.
a: toes: the three long parts pointing forward
web of skin: the thin skin between the toes
pushes water this way: backwards, behind the duck
items.why: The web of skin between the toes makes the foot a wide paddle. The duck pushes water backwards, and the water pushes the duck forward.
items.art: A drawing of a duck's foot spread open, with two label lines and one empty arrow.

items.p: A snake's skin is slimy.
items.why: False. A snake's skin is dry and covered in scales. Earthworms and snails are slimy. Snakes only look shiny.

items.p: A cow has no top front teeth. Instead she has a hard ________ of gum.
items.why: A cow holds grass between her bottom front teeth and the hard pad of gum on top, then tears the grass off.

items.p: Match each animal to what they push on to move.
items.why: Fliers push on air, swimmers push on water, and walkers, runners and crawlers push on the ground or the soil.

items.p: Three of these animals swallow food without chewing it. Which one chews?
items.why: A cow chews and grinds her food with flat molars. Snakes, kingfishers and frogs swallow their food whole.

items.p: A child has 20 milk teeth. A seven-year-old has lost 4 of them. How many milk teeth does the child still have?
items.why: 20 take away 4 is 16. The child still has 16 milk teeth. Big new teeth will grow where the 4 fell out.

items.p: Lakshmi and her brother Arjun live in Mysuru. They are talking about legs.

views.says: Having no legs is better. A snake can go into tiny holes and swim, and she never trips.
Having legs is better. With legs you can run fast and jump over things.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, and says what the other side has right. For example: legs let you jump a ditch, but a snake can slide into a narrow crack where legs would get in the way.
items.why: Every body is good for some places and not others. A strong answer gives at least one real thing that each body can do.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: many people think that bigger animals always jump farther. What would you test to find out if that is true?
items.a: I would ask a big person and a small person to jump from the same line in the same way, three times each, and measure. I could also look up how far a grasshopper jumps compared to her body length.
items.why: A strong answer describes a fair test: the same start line, the same way of jumping, more than one try, and a measurement. It may also say that tiny animals like grasshoppers jump many times their own length.

items.p: Your arm and a bat's wing have the same bones: one long upper bone, then two bones side by side, then small wrist bones, then finger bones. Draw your arm and a bat's wing side by side. Colour the same bones the same colour.
items.a: An arm and a bat wing, each with one long upper bone, two lower bones, small wrist bones and long finger bones in the wing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same pattern in both: one bone, then two, then wrist bones, then fingers. The bat's fingers are very long to hold the skin of the wing.
items.art: An empty box split into two halves.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: invent an animal who lives in a pond and eats seeds that float on the water. How does the animal move, and what does the mouth look like?
items.a: My animal has webbed feet to paddle, and a short, thick beak with comb-like edges to scoop up floating seeds and crack them.
items.why: A strong answer gives the animal a body part that pushes on water, such as webbed feet or fins, and a mouth that fits seeds, such as a short, thick beak.

items.p: Where would a snake have the hardest time moving?
items.why: A snake moves by pushing the curves of her body against bumps. Smooth glass has almost no bumps to push on, so a snake slides about and moves slowly. A rough doormat gives her plenty to push on.

items.p: Who jumps farthest for their own body size? Put these in order, from the shortest jump to the longest: an elephant, you, a grasshopper.
items.why: An elephant cannot jump at all. You can jump about as far as your own height, or a little less. A grasshopper can jump many times the length of their own body.

items.p: A bat's wing has the same kinds of bones as your arm and hand.
items.why: True. A bat's wing has one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones and very long finger bones. The skin of the wing is stretched between the fingers.

items.p: Label the bird's wing on the way down and on the way up: wide and flat, bent in.
labels: wing on the way down: wide and flat
wing on the way up: bent in
a: wide and flat: on the way down, pushing a lot of air
bent in: on the way up, pushing less air
items.why: On the way down, the wing spreads wide and flat to push a lot of air down. On the way up, many birds bend the wing in, so it pushes less air the wrong way. In Wing Push, your notebook did the same: flat it pushed a lot of air, and edge first it pushed very little.
items.art: Two drawings of a crow from the side, one with the wing spread down and one with the wing bent in and up, each with an empty label line.

items.p: An animal who eats both plants and other animals is called an ________.
items.why: Crows, sloth bears and most humans eat both plants and animals, so they are omnivores.

items.p: Match each glider to how the glider spreads out.
pairs: Skin flaps held out on long ribs
The whole body made flat and wide
Big fins spread out like wings
items.why: Each glider makes a wide, flat shape, which pushes on a lot of air and slows the fall.

quiz.p: How does an earthworm move without legs?
opts: By stretching and squeezing the body, while tiny bristles grip the soil
quiz.why: An earthworm makes her body long and thin, then short and fat, one part at a time. Tiny bristles grip the soil so she does not slide back. If you said jumping, think of the frog: jumping needs legs.

quiz.p: What do a bird's wings push on to hold the bird up?
quiz.why: Wings push air down, and the air pushes the wings up. In Wing Push, you felt this when the flat notebook was hard to swing.

quiz.p: Why do a frog's back legs fold up in a Z shape when she sits?
opts: So they can straighten fast and give a long push when she jumps
quiz.why: Folded legs are ready to straighten. Long, folded legs push on the ground for a long time, so the frog jumps far.

quiz.p: Which teeth grind food into small bits?
quiz.why: Molars are wide and bumpy, and grind food. Incisors cut, and canines grip and tear. If you picked the front teeth, remember the cucumber bite in My Teeth Map: your front teeth made cuts, not mush.

quiz.p: A tiger has very long pointed canines. What does a tiger eat?
quiz.why: Long canines grip and tear meat. A tiger is a carnivore. Grass-eaters like cows have wide, flat grinding teeth instead.

quiz.p: Which bird has a beak made for cracking seeds?
opts: A sparrow, with a short, thick beak
A kingfisher, with a long, sharp beak
A sunbird, with a long, curved beak
quiz.why: A short, thick beak is strong enough to crack seeds. A kingfisher's beak grabs fish, and a sunbird's beak reaches nectar.

quiz.p: Why does a duck have skin between her toes?
opts: To push a lot of water back when she swims
quiz.why: The web of skin makes the foot a wide paddle. The duck pushes water back, and the water pushes her forward.

quiz.p: Which of these animals moves mostly with fins?
quiz.why: A rohu fish swims with a tail fin and steers with side fins. A crow flies with wings, and a gecko runs and climbs on four legs.

quiz.p: A duck's beak is wide and flat, with tiny comb-like edges. What are the edges for?
opts: To let water out and keep food in
quiz.why: A duck scoops up water with food in it. The comb-like edges let the water out and keep the small bits of food in.

quiz.p: What does a snake push on to move forward?
opts: Stones, sticks and bumps on the ground
quiz.why: A snake pushes the curves of her body sideways against bumps on the ground. In the Snake Wiggle, the cushions gave you something to push on.

quiz.p: A cow has no top front teeth. How does her jaw move when she chews grass?
opts: Far from side to side, so her molars grind
quiz.why: A cow's jaw swings from side to side, so her flat molars rub the grass into a mush. In the Press or Grind test, rubbing broke the leaf much more than pressing did.

open_questions.q: Why did some fish first come out of the water and walk?
open_questions.why_open: Long ago, some fish with bony, fleshy fins began to move on land. Scientists still argue about why: to find food, to escape hunters, or to move between drying pools.

open_questions.q: Why do some birds hop and others walk?
open_questions.why_open: Sparrows mostly hop, pigeons walk, and crows do both. Scientists have ideas, but there is no clear answer yet.

maths.problem: In the Jump Test, a child's longest straight-legged jump was 2 foot-lengths. The longest big-bend jump was 5 foot-lengths. How many foot-lengths farther was the big-bend jump?
maths.explain: Count up from 2 to 5: 3, 4, 5. That is 3 more. So the big-bend jump was 3 foot-lengths farther.
maths.context: This is about the Jump Test, where you jumped with straight legs, a small bend and a big bend.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two numbers shows how much bending the knees helped.

maths.problem: A frog jumps across the kitchen floor. Each jump covers 3 tiles. After 4 jumps, how many tiles has the frog crossed?
maths.explain: Each jump is 3 tiles. 3, 6, 9, 12. After 4 jumps, the frog has crossed 12 tiles.
maths.context: This is about a frog making jumps of the same length, one after another.
maths.why_maths: When every jump is the same length, counting in equal groups tells us how far the frog went.

maths.problem: A child counts the teeth in the mirror. There are 10 teeth on top and 8 on the bottom, because 2 bottom teeth fell out. How many teeth does the child have now? How many will there be when the 2 new teeth grow in?
maths.answer: 18 teeth now, and 20 when the 2 new ones grow.
maths.explain: 10 and 8 make 18. When 2 new teeth grow in, 18 and 2 make 20.
maths.context: This is about the Teeth Map activity, where you counted your own teeth in a mirror.
maths.why_maths: Adding the top and bottom rows tells us how many teeth there are in all, and adding again helps us predict.

maths.problem: In Message Relay, each animal can carry the message twice. There are 8 animals. What is the largest number of turns the animals can carry the message in one game?
maths.explain: Each of the 8 animals can go twice. 8 and 8 make 16. There are only 12 places, so the team has 4 turns to spare, but only if they choose carefully.
maths.context: This is about the Message Relay game, where the team chooses an animal for each place.
maths.why_maths: Working out the turns in advance helps the team plan, so the ant and the gecko are not used up before the ceiling card comes up.

science: Jumping: take-off speed depends on how hard and for how long the legs push on the ground (impulse); a counter-movement or crouch lengthens the push. Standard biomechanics.
Frog jumping: long hind limbs folded in three segments; Astley and Roberts, Biology Letters, 2012, on elastic energy storage in frog jumps.
Grasshopper and locust jumping: energy stored in the hind legs and released at once (catapult mechanism); Bennet-Clark, Journal of Experimental Biology, 1975.

Bird take-off: the legs give most of the starting speed; Earls, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2000 (starlings and quail); Provini and others, Journal of Experimental Biology, 2012 (zebra finches and diamond doves).

Snake lateral undulation pushes against irregularities in the ground; snakes move poorly on smooth surfaces. Gray and Lissmann, Journal of Experimental Biology, 1950; Hu and others, PNAS, 2009, on belly scales.
Duck paddling: toes spread on the power stroke and fold on the recovery stroke. Any zoology textbook.
Draco dussumieri, the southern flying lizard of the Western Ghats; Chrysopelea ornata, the ornate flying snake of India, flattens the body to glide.
Ruminant dentition: no upper incisors, a dental pad, side-to-side grinding; carnivore carnassials and a mainly up-and-down jaw. Rodent incisors grow throughout life. Elephant tusks are incisors.
Human teeth: 20 primary teeth, 32 permanent teeth including wisdom teeth; front primary teeth usually shed between about 6 and 8.
Homologous forelimbs of tetrapods (humerus, radius and ulna, carpals, digits). Any biology textbook.

Darwin's finches: Darwin at the Galápagos in 1835; John Gould identified them as finches in 1837; Peter and Rosemary Grant, Daphne Major from 1973, and the 1977 drought (Boag and Grant, Science, 1981).
Origin of bird flight: arboreal ('trees down') and cursorial ('ground up') hypotheses; wing-assisted incline running in chukar partridges, Dial, Science, 2003.
Sloth bear (Melursus ursinus) diet of termites, ants and fruit.
Tirukkural 490, chapter 49 'Knowing the fitting time'; Tao Te Ching chapter 76.

roots.context: We have tested our own jumps, flapped like a bird, wiggled like a snake and ground leaves like a cow. Now we ask what the Jump Test tells us about moving, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Jump Test, you jumped only a short way with straight legs, but much farther with knees well bent. Your feet push on the floor only while your legs straighten. A bigger bend gives a longer push, so you leave the floor faster. So a jump is made on the ground, before you ever leave it.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a jump as the flying part, through the air. But once your feet leave the floor, nothing more can push you. The whole jump was made in the short push before, while you still touched the ground.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Jump Test, straight-legged jumps went only a little way, and jumps with a big knee bend went much farther. A frog's long back legs fold up in a Z, so her push on the ground lasts a long time.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who jumps the same way a frog does: bend first, then push.
three.what_is_life: Every moving animal is always pushing on something: the ground, the water or the air.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of bodies shaped for different pushes: legs, wings, fins and webbed feet. It is also full of mouths shaped for different foods.

roots.thread: Your arm, a bat's wing, a frog's leg and a whale's flipper look very different. Inside, they are built from the same set of bones: one bone, then two bones, then small wrist bones, then fingers. All these animals came from the same long-ago fish with bony, fleshy fins. One plan of bones has grown into jumping legs, flapping wings, paddling flippers and your own hands. And each of them moves by pushing on the same ground, water and air that we all share.

teachings.teaching: Tiruvalluvar says: when the time is not right, wait still, like a heron. When the right moment comes, strike quickly, like a heron striking a fish.
teachings.link: A heron, a kingfisher and a frog all wait very still, ready, and then move in one fast strike or push. The waiting, with legs or neck bent, is part of the move.

teachings.teaching: Laozi says that living things are soft and bendable, and dead things are stiff and hard. What is stiff will break. What is soft and bendable will last.
teachings.link: In the Jump Test, stiff, straight legs pushed only a little. Bent legs, ready to straighten, gave the longest jumps. Your legs could push only because they could bend.

science.text: A jump's length is set by how fast the body leaves the ground, and that depends on how hard and how long the legs push.
The limbs of birds, bats, frogs, whales and humans are built from the same set of bones, because these animals share ancestors.
A frog chooses when to jump: she watches, waits and decides. How much a frog feels and knows as she does this is still an open question for science.

other_view.view: A frog's fast escape jump is mostly a reflex: nerves in the body and brain set off the jump very quickly, without the frog stopping to think. In this view, choosing belongs to slower actions, like hunting.

practice.title: Crouch Like a Heron
practice.say: Stand with your feet a little apart. Bend your knees, as if you are about to jump. Stay there, very still, like a heron by the water. Breathe in slowly, and out slowly, three times. Feel your legs ready to push. Now, very slowly, straighten your legs and stand tall. Did you feel the push in your legs, even slowly?
practice.kid: Bend your knees, ready to jump. Stay still like a heron. Breathe slowly three times. Feel your legs, ready. Now stand up very slowly.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1835, Charles Darwin visited the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific Ocean. He collected many small brown birds. Their beaks were very different. Some were thick and strong, and some were thin and pointed. Darwin thought they were different kinds of birds, such as wrens, blackbirds and finches. Back in England in 1837, the bird expert John Gould looked at them closely. He found that they were all finches, close relatives of each other. Their beaks fitted different foods: big seeds, small seeds or insects. Darwin came to think that beaks change over many, many generations. He thought this was far too slow for anyone to watch. Then, in 1973, Rosemary Grant and Peter Grant began to measure every finch on Daphne Major, one tiny island. In 1977 almost no rain fell. The small, soft seeds ran out, and only big, hard seeds were left. Most of the finches died. Finches with deeper, stronger beaks could crack the big seeds, so more of them lived. Their chicks had bigger beaks too. The Grants had watched beaks change in just a few years.
how_we_found_out.who: Charles Darwin and John Gould, then Rosemary Grant and Peter Grant
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Darwin first thought the birds with different beaks were different kinds of birds, not all finches. He also thought beaks change far too slowly for anyone to see.

Followed every experiment, activity and the project step by step in a flat: made the snake and leaf results honest, added the colours, and removed a bird-watching step that repeated Take-off Watch. Cut repeated drawings and questions, fixed a wrong status on the bird take-off claim, a toothpaste line in the story, and a teeth-count mismatch, and kept 9 real jokes.

quiz: A frog's folded back legs straighten fast to push her off the ground.
Long back legs fold up while resting and push hard against the ground when they straighten.
Birds take off using only their wings.
Many birds get most of their starting speed from a jump with their feet.
When a leg pushes back on the ground, the body moves forward.
The ground pushes back on the leg, so the body is pushed forward and up.
Animals with big, sharp teeth eat only meat.
The Indian sloth bear has big canines but eats mostly termites, ants and fruit.
A snake's skin is wet and slimy.
A snake's skin is dry and covered in scales; earthworms and snails are the slimy ones.
A bat's wing and a whale's flipper are built from the same set of bones.
Many limbs share one bone plan, shaped differently for flying, swimming, jumping or holding.
Bigger animals always jump farther.
A tiny flea jumps many body-lengths, but an elephant cannot jump at all.
A cow's wide, bumpy back teeth are good for grinding grass.
Molars grind food into small bits, and plant eaters need to grind tough plants.
A gliding animal stays in the air by flapping hard and fast.
A glider spreads out a flat body and falls slowly forward through the air without flapping.
A fish swims by pushing water backwards with the tail and fins.
When a fish pushes water back, the water pushes the fish forward.
odd: Fins, webbed feet and flippers push on water to swim; a beak is a mouth for getting food.
Cows, goats and buffaloes eat plants and have grinding teeth; a tiger eats meat and has tearing canines.
An arm, a bat wing and a flipper share one bone plan; a butterfly wing has no bones inside.
Earthworms, snakes and leeches have no legs and push with their bodies; a rabbit pushes with legs.
Frogs, grasshoppers and kangaroos jump with long back legs; an elephant cannot jump at all.
